questions.question: What HTTP method is used to update an existing asset in Orchestrator?
options: POST
PUT
PATCH
UPDATE
questions.explanation: PUT is used to update assets in Orchestrator. The full endpoint is PUT /odata/Assets({asset_id}) with the complete asset object in the request body.

questions.question: Why do you need the asset ID when updating an asset?
options: To authenticate the request
To specify which asset to update (required in endpoint path)
IDs are not needed; use asset name instead
For logging purposes only
questions.explanation: The asset ID is required in the endpoint path: PUT /odata/Assets({asset_id}). While you can filter by name to get the ID first, the update operation itself requires the numeric ID.

questions.question: When updating an asset, which field contains the new value for Text/Bool/Integer assets?
options: NewValue
Value
Data
AssetValue
questions.explanation: The 'Value' field contains the updated value for Text, Bool, and Integer assets. For Credential assets, use 'CredentialUsername' and 'CredentialPassword' fields instead.

questions.question: How do you update only the password of a Credential asset?
options: Send PUT request with only CredentialPassword field
Send complete asset object with new CredentialPassword value
Use PATCH with CredentialPassword field only
Credential passwords cannot be updated via API
questions.explanation: PUT requires the complete asset object. To update a credential password, send the full asset with the updated CredentialPassword field. The username and all other fields must be included even if unchanged.

questions.question: Can you change an asset's scope (e.g., from Global to Per Folder) via API update?
options: Yes, by updating the ValueScope field
No, scope is immutable after creation
Yes, but only from Global to Per Folder, not reverse
Yes, by changing OrganizationUnitId field
questions.explanation: Asset scope (ValueScope) cannot be changed after creation via API. To change scope, you must delete the asset and recreate it with the new scope. This is a design limitation to prevent accidental scope changes.

questions.question: What's the correct pattern for updating an asset value?
options: Get asset by name → Modify Value field → PUT with modified object
POST to /odata/Assets/Update with new value
PATCH /odata/Assets with asset name and new value
DELETE old asset → POST new asset with same name
questions.explanation: Correct pattern: (1) GET the asset by name to retrieve current object and ID, (2) Modify the Value field in the object, (3) PUT the modified object to /odata/Assets({id}). This ensures all required fields are preserved.

questions.question: What happens if two processes try to update the same asset simultaneously?
options: Orchestrator queues updates sequentially
Last write wins; no conflict detection
Both updates fail with conflict error
Orchestrator merges the changes
questions.explanation: Last write wins - there's no built-in conflict detection or locking. If two processes update simultaneously, the second PUT request will overwrite the first. For critical updates, implement application-level locking or coordination.

questions.question: When updating an asset, which fields are required in the PUT request body?
options: Only Name and Value
Only Value and ValueType
All fields from the original asset object
Name, Value, and ValueScope
questions.explanation: PUT requests require the complete asset object with all fields. Best practice: GET the asset first, modify only the necessary fields (e.g., Value), then PUT the entire object back. Missing required fields will cause the update to fail.

questions.question: What validation should you perform before updating an asset?
options: No validation needed; Orchestrator validates everything
Check asset exists, validate new value type matches asset type
Only check if user has permission
Validation is optional for updates
questions.explanation: Always validate: (1) Asset exists (GET succeeds), (2) New value type is compatible (e.g., don't assign string to Integer asset), (3) Value meets business constraints. While Orchestrator does some validation, client-side validation prevents errors and provides better error messages.

questions.question: What's a common use case for programmatically updating assets?
options: Changing configuration based on runtime conditions
Rotating credentials on a schedule
Storing process results for the next run
All of the above
questions.explanation: All are valid use cases: (1) Dynamic config based on conditions (e.g., enable/disable features), (2) Automated credential rotation for security, (3) Stateful processing (storing last processed ID, timestamps). Assets provide flexible, centralized storage for mutable configuration.
